utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Karadzic remains absent from these proceedings and has communicated to the Chamber once again that this is because he considers himself not to be adequately prepared. As I stated earlier on, the Trial Chamber considers Mr. Karadzic's absence as the voluntary waiver of his right to attend the trial, and therefore the Chamber will continue hearing the Prosecution's opening statement. Mr. Tieger, you may now proceed with the rest of your opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. We resume today with the shelling and sniping campaign against Sarajevo's civilian population. Having already discussed the nature and duration of the campaign, the weapons used, the command and control structure, the orders by the accused to halt the campaign now and then when it suited his purposes. And the evidence is clear, Your Honours, that the accused knew throughout the course of the 44-month siege that his forces were shelling and sniping at civilians and creating conditions of terror for the citizens of Sarajevo. For example, his opportunistic orders to halt shelling reveal not only his command and control but also his awareness of the nature of the campaign. Recall, for example, the order he issued in July 1993 that we saw the other day when there appeared to be an opportunity to cut a deal to ethnically partition Bosnia. As a result, he directed the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to cease what had been happening, that is, "the unnecessary and uncontrolled firing on Sarajevo." Another example is an order the accused issued on the 7th of February, 1994, just two days after a Bosnian Serb shell had killed 61 people at the Markale market in Sarajevo. The Markale shelling occurred in the context of a particularly intensive period of shelling. In the first two weeks of January 1994 alone, United Nations military observers recorded over 6600 shells impacting in Bosnian government controlled Sarajevo. Now, these attacks generated an international outcry and further pressures from the international community, culminating in the threat of air-strikes to deter further bombardments by the Bosnian Serbs. And in the face of this pressure, Karadzic decided it was necessary to curtail the campaign. "There is evidence to suggest that Serbs are not responding in equal measure to Muslim artillery provocations - sometimes 20 to 30 or even 70 times more. The international community does not object to us responding, only the scale of retaliation is many times too great. In addition, the Muslims are provoking us into wasting our ammunition." And Karadzic ordered: "... the strictest possible control ..." and to respond "only against military targets" and only in "equal measure" and to "exclude the possibility of uncontrolled shelling." Again, Your Honours, in exercising his command authority for the purpose of serving perceived Serb interests, in this instance to moderate international pressure, Karadzic revealed both his control over the forces and his knowledge of the indiscriminate and disproportionate shelling and shelling against non-military targets. But even without his orders, the evidence demonstrates clearly that the accused knew of civilian targeting by his forces because for the duration of the siege, UNPROFOR and members of the international community repeatedly told him that it was happening. For example, the United Nations chief military observer, after the indiscriminate bombardments of Sarajevo at the end of 1992, complained directly to Karadzic as well as to Plavsic and Mladic, only to be told that this type of fire was legitimate and that they were defending Serbs. Or this letter from the commander of UNPROFOR, that is the United Nations Protection Force, to the accused in October 1994 regarding sniping: "These incidents are a crime against humanity." And he goes on to say: "... are in direct violation of the agreement to eliminate sniping activities in the Sarajevo region, signed on August 14th 1994." "Immediately take additional measures to ensure that there is no recurrence of these against innocent civilians." The military assistant to General Morillon in 1992 and 1993 recalls that General Morillon repeatedly telling Karadzic and Mladic at various meetings during his time in Bosnia that world history would judge them and the Bosnian Serbs by the way they were using their artillery against cities, towns, and defenceless civilians and that they had to stop. Karadzic's political allies in Belgrade also knew what was going on in Sarajevo and considered it both politically unsound and criminal, beginning with Slobodan Milosevic, who described the earliest bombardments as "bloody criminal." And you see in this slide a code cable following a talk with President Milosevic in which he indicates precisely that. In any event, Your Honours, the accused, like the rest of the world, knew about the Bosnian Serb attacks on civilians in Sarajevo from any number of sources, from the media, from newspapers, satellite television, all of which reported the shelling and sniping regularly and sometimes daily around the world. And I'd like to show you just a small example of the kind of information that was available to everyone, including the accused at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Dusk in Sarajevo. Amongst the city's ancient minarets the rockets fall, heralding another night of heavy shelling."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "In Sarajevo, the crossroads can be lethal, need to be taken at speed. They and the avenues that cut across the city offer the Serb gunners in the hills above with open lines of fire. Prime targets which the old and the infirm are forced to accept as the new uncomfortable realities of life."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Sarajevo's burning, in its heart and in its suburbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Zijad Kajindjic [phoen] is alive because he decided to listen to the 4.00 news last Friday afternoon. He left his family sheltering in the cellar and, with his son Muris, went upstairs. While the news was on, the house was hit by a tank round. This morning Mr. Kajindjic buried his wife, his daughter, two of his grandchildren, and a friend who'd come around to their house with some aspirin. The graveyard was shelled while they were there. "There isn't a time or a place where the citizens of Sarajevo can feel safe. Some parts of the city are more dangerous than others, but the shelling is indiscriminate and it kills people every day."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "The lives of the people of Sarajevo get more difficult all the time. At least half the city is without water. A tap in a burnt-out kiosk near the ruins of the railway station has shorter queues than most because it is overlooked by a sniper. Guns fired with intent to kill are so much a part of the daily routine here that they hardly notice."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Even by the crazed standards of Sarajevo, the horrendous night. Each luminous blob deadly and indiscriminate. Deafening and relentless artillery and mortar fire, speckled with machine-gun and rifle bullets. In the dark places below are over 300.000 citizens enduring a Serbian onslaught possibly in retaliation for an attempt by the Bosnians to break out from the siege in the past few days."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "This is supposed to be a safe area in the making. There was supposed to be a cease-fire but the shelling has been getting worse for the last 48 hours, and today the people of Sarajevo suffered as much as on any day in this war."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "When the war was starting, sniping like this would have sent them to their cellars. These days it's different. They know how to take cover, when to wait, and when to run. It's still terrifying and deadly, but like fetching water, it's part of the daily grind."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "In Sarajevo, the horrors are not just heard of but lived through day by day. This a particularly heavy bombardment of the old city. A single artillery shell fell on a queue of people waiting to pick up water outside the brewery. Eight were killed and 18 seriously injured. Of the dead, three came from one family, the mother and father who were killed instantly and the daughter ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "The UN command was dispensing calm assurance but it wasn't being felt at street level just afterwards, where people were fleeing from yet another sniper attack. We asked one of them how long it had been going on. Two and a half years, he said."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "The efforts to cling to a kind of normality in Sarajevo are being undermined. Not yet driven underground and into shelters, much of the population is at risk, as this morning, a shell landing among people walking near the Holiday Inn. With only the occasional random lethal explosion, people are still walking to work, queuing for food or attending their allotments, taking a chance. But this morning, five were injured, two seriously, and there's been sniper fire around the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a small reflection, Your Honours, of the campaign against the civilians of Sarajevo. Yet, despite knowing that his troops were targeting civilians, despite frequent protests from international military personnel and diplomats, despite the repeated condemnations from the international community and the world's media, the accused, apart from sporadic curtailments to achieve some momentary advantage, took no steps to prevent the continuation of the shelling and sniping of civilians and did not take steps to punish those responsible. Far from preventing the ongoing crimes committed by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps against the civilian population of Sarajevo or from punishing or dismissing senior members of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps responsible for those crimes, the accused in fact promoted them. On the 16th of December, 1992, the accused "exceptionally promoted the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps Commander Stanislav Galic to the rank of major-general." On the 24th of March, 1994, the accused exceptionally promoted then deputy-commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps Dragomir Milosevic to major-general. On the 7th of August, 1994, the accused granted an early promotion to retiring commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps Stanislav Galic, making him lieutenant-general. On the 28th of June, 1994, the accused exceptionally promoted Ratko Mladic to the rank of colonel-general. Your Honours, as supreme commander of the armed forces, and in particular in this instance of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, Radovan Karadzic led a campaign of shelling and sniping that struck civilians and civilian objects all over Sarajevo, day after day for 44 months. This shelling targeted at civilians, indiscriminate and disproportionate, and the targeting of civilians by snipers had no military purpose. That ongoing attack on civilians who were already rendered vulnerable by privation and isolation was designed to terrorise them, an intent made more obvious with every passing day. The scale, duration, consistency, and pattern of the shelling and sniping alone demonstrate that the shelling and sniping was the intended product of a tight command and control structure headed by Radovan Karadzic. The orders issued, the accused's opportunistic modulation of the campaign, Karadzic's routine defence of the campaign in the face of constant condemnation further demonstrate the inescapable conclusion that for 44 months Karadzic directed a campaign of terror against a civilian population who were targeted for living in the capital of a multi-ethnic country that he sought to ethnically separate. Your Honours, I turn next to Count 11, the taking of hostages in May of 1995 through June of 1995, which further reveal the accused's disregard of the law in pursuit of his view of the Serbian interests. As the shelling and sniping continued, an increasingly alarmed international community attempted to engage in efforts to deter the attacks on civilians. On the 24th of May, 1995, Bosnian Serb forces removed weapons from weapons collection points in Sarajevo, and despite a demand by the UNPROFOR commander to return them, failed to do so. His demand was predicated upon his concern that the weapons would continue to be used on the populated areas of Sarajevo. As I say, those weapons were not returned, and on the 25th of May, NATO carried out an air-strike on a bunker in an ammunition dump outside Pale. The next day, Bosnian Serb forces began to take hostage United Nations military observers in various locations. Now, as the Court may be aware, United Nations military observers were unarmed observers of the warring factions who were responsible for liaison between the warring parties and also between the parties and UNPROFOR. Ultimately, over 200 United Nations military observers and UNPROFOR peacekeepers, men from many different countries, were taken and held hostage between the 26th of May and the 19th of June. Some hostages were handcuffed to flagpoles or a radar dome or lightning rods. Others were placed under force between radar antennas. Some were physically abused. Bosnian Serb forces -- and we can see a brief clip of that. Just a handful of the men who were taken and held hostage and used, as you can see, as human shields. In addition, Bosnian Serb forces also shelled all the safe areas on the 26th of May, including Tuzla, where 71 people were killed in the market-place. The accused, Your Honours, had previously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are hearing French, so let's try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the accused had previously made very clear that he was prepared to use UN personnel as weapons to coerce the international community. Asked in 1994 about the possibility that President Clinton might lift the arms embargo and provide the Muslims with arms, he said that, among other things: "We would take the 'Blue Helmets' hostages ... for the benefit of our people, we will do anything we have to do, without mercy." Indeed, in April and November 1994, UN personnel had been taken hostage by Bosnian Serb forces in response to NATO air-strikes. And in 1995, in the weeks immediately preceding the taking of hostages in May, the accused re-affirmed the threat to take hostages. First in a meeting with UNPROFOR Commander Smith on the 10th of May, 1995, Karadzic made clear that in the event of a NATO attack, the UN would be treated as enemies, saying, "we would treat you as the enemy." Then, just a few days before the hostage-taking, Karadzic echoed the threat saying: "If NATO were to attack, they would be taken hostages, if they were to attack, they would be our enemy ... if NATO attacked us, we would consider the UN our enemy." But again, Your Honours, let's hear directly from the accused what happened and why because he explained it at the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 14th and 15th of June, 1995, and I want to turn your attention to what he said. Both his determination to dramatise the situation by ordering a removal of weapons and then ordering the taking of the hostages. "I must say that we decided to opt for an aggravation of the situation, and the Supreme Command and I as the commander and with the Main Staff, we agreed that the worst for us is a war of low intensity, long duration, et cetera, and that we have to heat up the situation, take whatever we can, create a fiery atmosphere and dramatise, threaten an escalation, et cetera, because we noticed that whenever we advance on Gorazde, on Bihac, or elsewhere, or if the situation escalates around Sarajevo, then the internationals come and diplomatic activity speeds up. We did that around Sarajevo, we took these artillery pieces, there are four artillery pieces, maybe they weren't crucial, but they resulted in the well-known bombing that unfortunately caused us material damage because we didn't disperse these weapons ..." And then he continued: "We ordered the arrest. We didn't go into detail as to when they would be tied up but it had a good effect. It was very shocking for the world. Now it's easy, when they ask us if that was a nice gesture, I ask if it's a nice gesture to bomb the Serbian rear and frighten our children and old people and force them to flee. Then nobody has a reply. So you don't respond with a response but with a counter-question, and they have nothing to say. As you know, this led to a horrible heating up, there were condemnations too, even from Yugoslavia, et cetera ... it showed them that if you, gentlemen, are going to do drastic measures, we will take drastic measures. There, mothers don't want to see their sons tied up like that, and a plane was shot down; God helped us in this case too." Similarly asked by a journalist whether it hadn't been a terrible mistake to "allow your people to capture UN soldiers to -- for the world to see them chained up, to see masked men holding guns to their heads, that's terrible. Isn't that an awful mistake?" Karadzic responded that: "One drastic move causes another drastic move ... we had to do something very drastic, you know, to prevent further strikes and in order to show to the national community that we are cornered and that being cornered are ready to defend ourselves by all means." Or as Momcilo Krajisnik would say simply at this same session that -- in June that I quoted from earlier, discussing an UNPROFOR request for a base in the Ilijas municipality in Sarajevo and its possible advantages to the Bosnian Serbs: "Truth be told, we sometimes do need to capture some hostages." And now, Your Honours, I move to the third major component of the case against Radovan Karadzic: His responsibility for one of humanity's dark chapters, the crimes committed to eliminate the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica. As I will discuss, Radovan Karadzic ordered the operation to take Srebrenica which was a culmination of his efforts to cleanse Eastern Bosnia. He was informed of its progress throughout by various means including Mladic, VRS reports, MUP reports, state security reports. He had direct contact with Mladic, maintained direct contact with his hand-selected civilian commissioner. He knew that the population was being moved out as it was happening. He ordered the removal of men from the area where there was a risk that they would be seen by the internationals. He knew that men were being killed. He covered up the mass expulsions and the murders and continues to do so to this day, and the only regret he had about the entire operation was that some Muslim men got away. And now I'd like to turn your attention to some of that evidence. Your Honours, Srebrenica was once simply the name of a small town and municipality in Eastern Bosnia. In 1991, just before the war, the population of Srebrenica municipality was 37.000, approximately 73 per cent of whom were Muslim. Srebrenica was known locally for its mining industry and health spas but hardly known outside of the former Yugoslavia. In July 1995, however, Srebrenica achieved worldwide infamy. In a matter of days, the entire Muslim population was forcibly removed from the Srebrenica enclave and more than 7.000 Muslim men and boys were murdered in a massive operation involving members of the VRS, the Bosnian Serb army; the MUP, the Bosnian Serb police; and civilian authorities. Within weeks, evidence of the mass executions began to emerge, including aerial images which showed areas of disturbed earth in locations where executions were thought to have taken place. And you can see two of those areas in the Orahovac area. In response, in September and October 1995, elements of the VRS, the army; of the police, the MUP; and civilian authorities conducted a massive clandestine operation to exhume the mass graves in Zvornik and Bratunac areas and move the corpses of those men to secondary grave-sites in an effort to conceal the crimes. During that process, the bodies of the victims were mangled, crushed, and separated by the heavy machinery used. I'll briefly show you a map of some of the primary and secondary grave-sites. It may not be immediately visible, but you can determine the number from this graphic. Your Honours, over 7500 persons have been reported as missing following the fall of Srebrenica, and to date more than 5.000 of those individuals had been exhumed from mass graves and identified through DNA testing. Your Honours, as I eluded to earlier and as we discussed the other day, the murder of these men and the mass expulsion of the women, children, and elderly did not arise from nowhere. These crimes were a culmination of the accused's determination to cleanse Eastern Bosnia, to ensure the Serb state that he envisioned. You will recall that I described the other day the adoption and implementation of the Strategic Objectives, beginning in May 1992, formalising objectives that were already being pursued, and the cleansing of Muslims in Eastern Bosnia. Now, you see before you the area covered by Strategic Objective 3 in Eastern Bosnia. Strategic Objective 3, a subset of Strategic Objective 1, which is separation; number 3 is the elimination of the Drina as a border separating Serbian states. That was promulgated, as you will recall, enunciated by the accused on May 12th, 1992. And we discussed the other day some of the actions that followed by the VRS combined with MUP forces. While much of Eastern Bosnia was conquered and cleansed by the latter part of 1992, there remained, nevertheless, some areas that Bosnian Serb force had not managed to conquer, including Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica. And you can see Srebrenica depicted in this graphic and the enclave of Zepa immediately below and Gorazde below that. And you can see the horseshoe area in red which reflects the areas under Bosnian Serb control and the otherwise clean area in Eastern Bosnia. On the 19th of November, 1992, the accused, through Mladic and the VRS Main Staff, issued Directive 4. Now, Your Honours, as you'll learn, a directive is a high command document which addresses broad issues of preparation and execution of military tasks or military operations for an extended period, setting out goals and tasks. Now, with respect to Eastern Bosnia, Directive 4 ordered the Drina Corps to cleanse the Muslim population from the areas of Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde. The Birac area is the area that includes Bratunac, Vlasenica, Zvornik, Srebrenica, and Cerska. I'd like to turn your attention to that order, to Directive 4, which states in significant part that the task of the Drina Corps shall be to: "... shall exhaust the enemy," and I'll quote now. "... shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population." This cleansing order was signed by General Mladic and was issued with Karadzic's full agreement and support. How do we know this? First, as before, turning to the accused himself because he acknowledged his awareness of and approval of the first seven directives. This is what he said in October 1995: " ... I have examined, approved, and signed seven directives. No one submitted the eighth and ninth to me." Now, Your Honours, as you will learn, this was correct in its essence but not its detail. Most directives do not appear to have been signed by the accused. This was in fact noted by General Mladic in April of 1995 when he too confirmed Karadzic's awareness and approval of the directives. And this is what Mladic said: "Some of these decisions were only presented to you, Mr. President. In others you participated as member of the Supreme Command. Some of the directives you signed, not all of them though. Before we constituted and oriented ourselves, I used to sign them." But beyond the accused's explicit acknowledgement of responsibility for the directive, beyond Mladic's confirmation of Karadzic's responsibility for Directive 4, the evidence also reveals Karadzic's strong and active interest in the implementation of Directive 4. On the 20th of November, 1992, the day after Directive 4 was issued, Mladic, at Karadzic's explicit request, issued an order to the Drina Corps to hold a military and political seminar three days later. "Pursuant to the request by the supreme commander [sic] of the Army of Republika Srpska (President of the Presidency, Dr. Radovan Karadzic) and with a view to carrying out timely preparation and holding a military and political seminar at the level of the Drina Corps, I hereby order ..." And he did so. Now, that order provided that Karadzic was to chair the seminar at which "the tasks for the corps in the days ahead" were to be discussed. In addition to chairing the meeting, the timetable issued for the meeting provided that Karadzic would give the opening and closing speeches and deliver the "tasks for further work for the Drina Corps and organs of civilian government." At that seminar held three days later, on the 23rd of November, 1992, the Drina Corps commander spoke about the further tasks of the Drina Corps, including tasks in the area of Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, and Cerska, the very same areas identified in Directive 4 from which the Muslim population was to be expelled. And the day after that meeting at which the supreme commander, Radovan Karadzic, was there for the purpose of delivering the tasks for the further work of the Drina Corps, the Drina Corps commander issued this order to the corps pursuant to Directive 4: "Launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." I should also note that beyond this explicit statement of the intent to cleanse the remaining Muslim population from the area, the order also stated the broader purpose of the operation when it identified the moral and psychological preparations to be conducted. And that's worth looking at briefly. You'll see it notes the moral and psychological operations [sic]: "Before initiating any kind of operation, inform the unit members about the important aim of the operation ... underline that the outcome of minor actions and of the whole operation is of a crucial importance for the realisation of the aim of the Serbian people, namely, the creation and establishment of a Serbian state in these areas." In short, Your Honours, beyond the accused's explicit acknowledgment of his responsibility for the first seven directives, including Directive 4, his hands-on involvement with his dissemination and implementation make crystal clear his responsibility for Directive 4 and the events that would follow. Beginning in early 1993, pursuant to that directive, pursuant to Directive 4 and the Drina Corps order we just saw, the Bosnian Serb army conducted a series of brutal and destructive military operations through the Kamenica, Cerska, and Konjevic Polje areas of Eastern Bosnia. And you can see those areas depicted on your screen, Your Honour. Just if you look toward the east you can see the bold indication of Bratunac, and above you'll see Konjevic Polje, Cerska to the left. This campaign, this military campaign, was characterised by the burning of Muslim houses and indiscriminate shelling of Muslim civilians. It resulted in the forcible transfer of tens of thousands of Bosnian Muslims from their homes in municipalities such as Bratunac, Vlasenica, and Zvornik, displacement from those homes to Muslim-held territory in and around Srebrenica and Zepa. Now, I want to turn your attention to just a few documents which illustrate nature of this brutal campaign. The first is an 8th February 1993 intercept between the Drina Corps commander and one of his subordinates. Drina Corps Commander Zivanovic: "Hold tightly the positions ... are the Turks' houses burning?" His subordinate: "They are burning, they are burning. "Zivanovic: Way to go, as many as possible." Next I'd like to turn your attention to a Birac Brigade combat report to the Drina Corps command on the 2nd of March, 1993: "Our forces which are moving in the wider area of Kamenica, Gajici, and Grobici worked according to plan without major problems. The village of Gobelji has been burnt, and tomorrow the plan is to do Paljevine." This combat report to the Drina Corps command was from now Lieutenant-Colonel Svetozar Andric, who, as a major back in May of 1992, had issued the order that you saw earlier which was that the moving out of the Muslim population must be organised and coordinated with the municipalities in which the moving is carried out. It specified that only women and children can move out, while men fit for military service were to be placed in camps for exchange. And that's an order that you saw on the first day. Your Honours, as these cleansings continued in 1993, the international community grew increasingly alarmed. A report issued on the 5th of May, 1993, by the UN Special Rapporteur of the Commission on Human Rights reflects the observations and awareness of the international community. "Massive and repeated violations of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 were perpetrated in recent combat in Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina. These were carried out by Serb forces in Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica in attacking and ambushing civilians attempting to flee their encirclement, in attacking the villages themselves ..." And during this time, the international community became similarly concerned by the humanitarian disaster unfolding within Srebrenica as tens of thousands of Bosnian Muslims who had been forcibly displaced from their homes in Eastern Bosnia by the operation we've just discussed and that we've seen reflected in some of those documents, as those people began to converge on Srebrenica, the population of the town swelled to between 50 and 60.000 people. I'd like to show you a brief video-clip which will provide some insight into the plight of those who had been cleansed and who sought some refuge in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "My first recollection is arriving at a village near Srebrenica, just to be totally engulfed by hundreds and hundreds of people. I thought I was standing in a movie and I kept expecting somebody to say, "Okay, cut,' and all these people with these gaunt, haunted faces and they all got expressionless faces. It's like life had drained out of them, you know, life is ebbing away. There was very little caring by the so-called authorities for the new arrivals. Nobody cared for the refugees. They were left for days on the street. No one cared anything about them. They arrived, you know, we followed a family through and they had been walking for something like 17 hours. You know, the mother carrying the little boy who'd been wounded by shrapnel in the hand. He had been wounded the same time as his father. They came, they didn't know where they were going. They had no relatives and no friends. "Where does this man recommend they can sleep? Where does this man recommend they can go? "I don't know where. This town has 60.000 refugees and there's only room for 10.000. Have you seen how many people are sleeping on the streets?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, following the direct intervention of UNPROFOR Commander Morillon, who himself went to Srebrenica in March of 1993 and was moved by the humanitarian disaster before him to famously assure the population that he would not abandon them, the United Nations Security Council, on April 16th, 1993, passed Resolution 819 which demanded that Srebrenica be treated as a "safe area." Resolution 819 condemned the actions of the Bosnian Serbs up to that point, stating that the Security Council: "Condemns and rejects the deliberate actions of the Bosnian Serb party to force the evacuation of the civilian population from Srebrenica and its surrounding areas as part of its overall abhorrent campaign of 'ethnic cleansing.'" Two days later, a cease-fire agreement was reached between the Bosnian army commander General Halilovic and the Bosnian Serb commander General Mladic in which they agreed that Srebrenica would be demilitarised. And less than a month later, on the 6th of May, 1993, the United Nations Security Council passed Resolution 824, which confirmed Srebrenica's status as a safe area and declared that Sarajevo, Tuzla, Zepa, Gorazde, and Bihac should also be treated as safe areas. The creation of these safe areas, in particular the Eastern Bosnian safe areas of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, provided the Muslim population with a degree of protection from the Bosnian Serb forces and temporarily forestalled the Bosnian Serbs' accomplishment of the goals set by Strategic Objective 1 and 3 and also the objective of Directive 4. However, both the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Muslims violated the safe area agreement, as you should note. Muslim forces in these enclaves, sometimes rag-tag and desperate, over time better armed, equipped, and trained, had engaged in attacks on Serb forces and also on Serb villages, killing civilians and destroying property. And even after the safe area agreement was reached, the Srebrenica enclave was never fully demilitarised. The Muslim forces only surrendered old and broken weapons while they kept working weapons. In addition, Bosnian helicopters flew in violation of the no-fly zone and delivered weapons to the enclave and to the Bosnian army. Thus, even after the declaration of the -- of Srebrenica as a safe area, attacks continued from within the enclave against the surrounding Serb areas. This intensified the level of animus in that area. On the part of the Bosnian Serbs, following the establishment of the safe area and the international condemnation you've seen, the previously overt and large-scale military operations to force out the Muslim population gave way to a more subtle strategy, that of rendering the UN forces ineffective by restricting their re-supply convoys, and simultaneously making life impossible for the Muslim inhabitants of the enclaves through shelling and sniping attacks and also through the restriction of humanitarian aid. The purpose of this more subtle strategy was to ensure that when conditions were right for the Bosnian Serb forces to make a final and decisive military assault on the enclaves, UNPROFOR's capacity to defend the Bosnian Muslims would be reduced and a broken Muslim population would flee from their tormentors. The ultimate goal of Directive 4 remained, that is, to breakthrough, take over, and expel the Muslims from the enclaves. I turn your attention here to a July 1994 report from the commander of the Bratunac Brigade to the members of his brigade, and this was sent after a visit by General Mladic. And it again expressly outlined the objective of a clean Drina and the strategy for achieving it. "We must attain our final goal - an entirely Serbian Podrinje. "We must continue to arm, train, discipline, and prepare the Republika Srpska army for the execution of this crucial task - the expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave. "There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave; we must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." And during that same year, in 1994, while the relatively subtle strategy was being pursued, prior to the final assault on Srebrenica both Karadzic and Mladic continued to voice strong views about what should happen to the Muslims. In July of 1994, Karadzic cast the goal in terms of reciprocating what the Bosnian government supposedly had in mind for the Serbs. And here's what he said: "We have to be ready to accept and be ready every day to make intensive life-and-death war, according to the wish of our enemy, until his complete defeat, or until our defeat and expulsion from these territories. In case of his victory, our enemy would not be generous nor merciful, but merciless and ready for our extinction." And therefore the Bosnian Serbs have to: "Accept the logic of our enemy," and as you can see from the previous passage, that logic was expulsion and extinction, and "defeat him mercilessly." As Mladic told the Assembly in January of 1994, referring to the enemy in Srebrenica among other places: "My concern is not that they will create the state. My concern is to have them vanish completely." The slow strangulation of the Srebrenica enclave continued. By early 1995, fewer and fewer supply convoys were making it through to the enclave. And on the 8th of March, 1995, Radovan Karadzic issued and signed Directive 7, to resolve the situation of the eastern enclaves. Directive 7 explicitly sets out the strategy for the VRS, the Bosnian Serb army, to make life unbearable for the Muslim populations of Srebrenica and Zepa through military action and through the restriction of aid and supply convoys to the enclaves. The tasks assigned to the Drina Corps, the operative corps in that area, were in part: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." This is Directive 7, issued and signed by the accused. And Directive 7 also outlined Karadzic's policy of preventing humanitarian aid from reaching the Muslim population and thereby disabling in addition UNPROFOR forces in the eastern enclaves while trying to minimise -- trying at the same time to accomplish this while minimising international condemnation. And Directive 7 ordered the state and military organs to: "Through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." Directive 7, Karadzic's order, was passed down the chain of command. On the 20th of March, 1995, the Drina Corps command drafted and sent an order to the brigade pursuant to Directive 7, repeating critical portions of Directive 7 word for word. "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Thus, Your Honours, pursuant to Directive 7, the already meager resources of the Muslim populations, which you saw earlier, were reduced even more. Even UNPROFOR forces stationed in the enclave, and those forces were DutchBat forces, the Dutch Battalion, started to run dangerously low on food, medicine, fuel, ammunition. The fuel situation grew so critical that DutchBat soldiers were forced to start patrolling on foot. In addition, in the months leading up to the enclave, Bosnian Serb army units stationed around Srebrenica shelled and sniped the enclave. Further efforts to make life unbearable and force the population to flee. By May 1995, the humanitarian situation in the enclave was dire. As ordered and envisioned by Directive 7. In early May, attack plans in line with Directive 7 were commenced by the Drina Corps but were almost immediately aborted due to lack of available resources, and that is forces, manpower. In early June 1995, the Drina Corps attacked and removed UNPROFOR forces from a UN observation point on the southern edge of the Srebrenica enclave and thereby gained control of a strategically important area which would serve as the staging area for the final attack on the enclave just a month later. In late June, Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik went to the Drina Corps command in Vlasenica. There they met with Radislav Krstic, who was then the deputy commander and Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, in order to advance the plan to attack Srebrenica and Zepa. Karadzic ordered Krstic or urged Krstic to make the attack happen as soon as possible. And on the 2nd of July, the commander of the Drina Corps issued a combat order code-named Krivaja 95. The Krivaja 95 order was issued pursuant to Directive 7 and ordered the Drina Corps to carry out offensive operations: "To split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica and to reduce them to their urban areas. "To create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves." The reduction of the already overcrowded enclaves to their small urban areas would intensify the already dire humanitarian situation in the towns that had been caused by the shelling, sniping, and restriction of humanitarian aid, a policy which was already making life unbearable for the Muslim population as intended. The attack on Srebrenica began on the 6th of July, 1995. Over the next few days, the Bosnian Serb army shelled civilians and civilian targets in the enclave. And you will hear from one of the United Nations military observers who was there about the intensity of the shelling and the resulting terror within the embattled Muslim population. In the days following the 6th of July, 1995, the five UNPROFOR observation posts in the southern part of the enclave fell one by one in the face of the advance by the Bosnian Serb forces. Let me show you just one of the UNMO reports, Your Honours, from July 7th, 1995, chronicling the Bosnian Serb army attack on Srebrenica. "The Bosnian Serb army offensive seems to be steadily intensifying. Whatever their aims are, they seem to be concentrating more on civ targets," that is civilian targets, "in Srebrenica town and Potocari. There are several civ cas," that is civilian casualties, "and unassessed damages to civ property. The team request action to be taken to stop this carnage and damage to civ property in a UN declared safe area." On the 9th of July, 1995, with no serious resistance from either the Muslim forces or the UNPROFOR forces in Srebrenica, the Bosnian Serb army leadership realised that it would feasible to now finish what had been put on hold in April of 1993, that is, the take-over of the enclave and the removal of the Muslim population. And in accordance with the military chain of command, the VRS sought and received agreement from the supreme commander, Radovan Karadzic, to expand the goal of the Krivaja 95 operation to include the actual take-over of the enclave. This is a 9 July 1995 Main Staff order. "The President of Republika Srpska has been informed of successful combat operations around Srebrenica by units of the Drina Corps and that they have achieved results which enable them to occupy the very town of Srebrenica." It continues: "The President of the Republic is satisfied with the results of the combat operations around Srebrenica and has agreed with the continuation of operations for the take-over of Srebrenica, disarming of Muslim terrorist gangs, and complete demilitarisation of the Srebrenica enclave." Now, this order, as you will see, Your Honours, also orders "full protection" to UNPROFOR and the Muslim civilian population, and orders the treatment of the civilian population and war prisoners in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. This cynically cosmetic or the nature of this lip service to international law is revealed not only by the very purpose of Directive 4 and Directive 7 to cleanse the population, but also by the events that would follow under the ultimate authority of the supreme commander. And so, pursuant to Karadzic's command, the command on July 9th, 1995, the take-over of the enclave and the long awaited cleansing of its Muslim population, another definitive step towards the full realisation of Strategic Objective 3 was finally underway. Srebrenica fell on the afternoon of July 11th, 1995. During the conquest of the town, Karadzic was kept informed of developments on the ground by Bosnian Serb army General Gvero, who reported to him, to Karadzic, concerning UNPROFOR complained -- complaints about attacks on UNPROFOR troops. He also assured Karadzic: "Everything is going according to plan, don't worry." A short time later, in the late afternoon, Gvero reported to Karadzic that the Serbian flag was flying above the Serbian church in Srebrenica. "President, Serbian silver, the Serbian church, the Serbian flag." And later that day, on the afternoon of 11 July, General Mladic and other VRS officers, including the commander of the Drina Corps Zivanovic and the Drina Corps Chief of Staff Krstic, walked through the empty streets of Srebrenica revelling in their victory. They were accompanied by a cameraman from the VRS Main Staff who recorded portions of that triumphant tour, including Mladic's chilling and prescient words. I'll show you that clip. At the end of this clip, Your Honours, you will see that it merges into the televised broadcast of those words by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Congratulations. "Congratulations, guys. Well done. "Are our guys still ahead? "They are. "Good. They are sweeping the town. It's taken. "You could easily have entered here by car, too. "Right, right. I know it's possible. Let it follow me slowly. "Come on, Zile. Come on, Zile. Krstic. Come on, Krle. "Film that flag of theirs, over there. Take the flag down so it doesn't wave. Stick it on the ground. Here so it can be filmed by the camera. Yes, yes, there you go. "Here we are, on the 11th of July, 1995, in Serb Srebrenica. On the eve of yet another great Serb holiday, we give this town to the Serb people as a gift. Finally, after the rebellion against the Dahis, the time has come to take revenge on the Turks in this region."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The time has come to take revenge on the Turks in this region, and you will learn, Your Honours, what happened to the men of Srebrenica by essentially following the fate of two groups. As the fall of Srebrenica became imminent, a group of approximately 15.000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys, with some women and children, gathered at the village of Susnjari, approximately 7 kilometres north-west of Srebrenica. These men, fearful about what would happen to them if they surrendered or were captured by Bosnian Serb forces, began to flee in a huge column through the woods toward Tuzla, a Bosnian Muslim-held area. Approximately one-third of that column was armed and the rest were unarmed soldiers and civilians. That's one group, and I'll return to them a bit later. A second group of Muslims consisting of thousands of women, children, and elderly, along with 1.000 to 2.000 Bosnian Muslim men, fled to the UNPROFOR compound in Potocari approximately 4 kilometres to the north of Srebrenica. There they sought the protection of UNPROFOR. And perhaps I can show you quickly a map depicting the -- that area and where Potocari is in relationship to Srebrenica. And you can see it there between -- on the road between Bratunac and Srebrenica. And if you look to the left, that's the area in which -- toward which the other column, the 15.000 men were fleeing. And you see that road there indicated by Kravica, Sandici, and so on, that's the area I'll be referring to later in which these men were later captured or surrendered. Your Honours, by the evening of the 11th of July, some 20 to 25.000 Bosnian Muslims had gathered in and around the UNPROFOR headquarters in Potocari. They were completely exhausted, had woefully insufficient access to food, water, basic medical treatment or even toilet facilities. The plan to "shrink the enclaves to the urban areas" had achieved its intended effect. These people were terrified, exhausted, and no longer with any hope of survival of a life in Srebrenica. On the day that Srebrenica fell, Radovan Karadzic moved forward quickly to cement the Bosnian Serbs' victory. On the 11th of July, he formally appointed Miroslav Deronjic who was president of the Bratunac SDS and one of Karadzic's proven and trustworthy ethnic cleansers from back in 1992. Appointed Deronjic as a civilian commissioner for the new Serbian municipality of Srebrenica. He also ordered the chief of the regional police headquarters to create a police station in Srebrenica and to work with Deronjic. Following the fall of Srebrenica, beginning on the evening of July 11th and continuing through to the morning of the 12th, Mladic held three meetings at the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac to discuss the fate of the Srebrenica enclave. The first meeting was with DutchBat. The second and third meetings were with DutchBat and with Muslim representatives. And during the course of the trial you will see portions of all three meetings. But here is a clip from the second meeting which was held on the evening of July 11th and it was the first one that was attended by a Muslim representative, a man named Nesib Mandzic. Mladic's words, as he threatens that Muslims will vanish, speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "In order to make a decision as a man and a commander, I need to have a clear position of the representatives of your people on whether you want to survive, stay, or vanish. I am prepared to receive here tomorrow, at 10.00 a.m., a delegation of officials from the Muslim side with whom I can discuss the salvation of your people from the enclave, the former enclave of Srebrenica. I shall order a cessation of operations until 10 a.m. tomorrow. If your fighters -- your fighters who lay down their arms we will treat in accordance with international conventions and we guarantee that everybody will live, even those who committed crimes against our people. Have I made myself clear? Nesib, the future of your people is in your hands, not only on this territory. I'm finished. You're free to go. I'll be waiting for you at 10.00 a.m. tomorrow. See them off."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mladic repeated this ultimatum at the third meeting, held the following morning. By this time, the Bosnian Serb army had received information about the Bosnian Muslim column of men attempting to flee out of the enclave, the column I mentioned to you before. During the third meeting he also announced, in a section that was either not filmed or later deleted from the film, that all men between the ages of 16 and 60 would be separated and screened for war crimes. And as I will explain shortly, no screening of any kind was conducted or intended. The men who were separated included some very young boys and elderly men above 70, and I'll talk to you about that shortly. But about the same time as the last meeting at Hotel Fontana on the morning of July 12th, Bosnian Serb army and Bosnian Serb police forces moved into Potocari. That's where the 20 to 25.000 Bosnian Muslims had gathered. Some Muslims were shot, others beaten and terrorised by Bosnian Serb forces, forces with no fear of apparent of consequences for doing so. Within hours of the expulsion of the Muslim population, those who would be allowed to live and those who were separated and murdered began. You will hear evidence, Your Honours, that Karadzic later suggested to journalists that Muslims were free to remain in Srebrenica if they wished, but like most of what he says about Srebrenica, nothing could be farther from the truth. Let's look at Mladic's contemporaneous remarks about who could stay and who could go. "Go ahead, General. "Mladic: Have these buses and trucks left?" His interlocutor: "They have." "Mladic: When?" His interlocutor: "Ten minutes ago. "Mladic: Good, excellent. Continue to monitor the situation. Don't let small groups of them sneak in. They've all capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all - those who want to and those who don't want to." For this purpose, buses from many surrounding municipalities were mobilised by the Main Staff through the Ministry of the Defence in Pale. This was a massive logistical operation that involved multiple municipalities and different Ministry of Defence departments. Women, children, and the elderly were expelled to Muslim-held territory in Kladanj. Meanwhile, all but a handful of the men and boys, that is, boys who looked roughly military age, were forcibly separated from their families and detained. The separation and detention of these men had nothing to do with any kind of "screening process." The Bosnian Serb army and Bosnian Serb police forces in Potocari separated and detained every man or boy who looked close to military age. No effort was made to distinguish soldiers from civilians. While a few military-aged men made it on to the first convoy, thereafter all the men were separated and detained. I would like to show you a bit of that separation and at the end you'll see some of the men who were being detained. [Video-clip played].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Wait, wait. Stay there, buddy. "It's all right. It's all right. "Come on, follow them there one by one. "No, no, you go there to the left, to the left. "Come on everyone, get in the column one by one." [Video-clip played].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Men are going this way and women are going that way. "This is no good. I'm talking about the overcrowding in this place, where all the men are being taken. They are sitting on each other. It's no good."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There are some people who tried to smuggle themselves onto a convoy and who are registered criminals."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mladic's false representation that they were separated to be screened for war crimes was intended only to mask the intended fate of these men. That pretense is revealed by any number of factors, including, one, there were no meaningful efforts of recording or listing of Muslim prisoners as they were taken into custody, as would have been the case if it was intended that they be imprisoned or exchanged. To the contrary, after being taken into custody, their personal identification documents were discarded or destroyed. In addition, their meager belongings contained in bags or rucksacks were put in piles and later burned. You saw some of those piles in the video we just saw. Further, no interrogation or questioning of the men and boys was conducted to detect possible criminals. In Potocari, these Muslim men and boys were not provided with any food, first aid, or medical care. And finally, once separated and taken to detention sites in Bratunac, they were packed into buildings to prevent them from being seen by air or by persons passing by. They were provided with no food, no first aid, no medical help, no hygiene, and many were brutally beaten and murdered. In one detention site alone more than 50 or more Muslim men were killed on the 12th and 13th of July. These circumstances, Your Honours, are unmistakable and the word "screening" in this context can take its place on the list of shameful euphemisms. In this case a euphemism for "marked for death." Your Honour, I note the time and I think in conformity with the schedule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, whenever it's convenient. We'll have a break of 25 minutes. --- Break taken at 3.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, on the 12th and 13th of July, 1995, about 25.000 Bosnian Muslim civilians were bussed outside the enclave of Srebrenica to the territory under Bosnian government control. As that operation progressed, the supreme commander, Radovan Karadzic, was advised that Krivaja 95 was going according to plan. As Mladic stated in the intercept of 12 July that we saw moments ago, the VRS was transferring all Muslim women, children, and elderly men, those who wanted to go and those who didn't. Just as envisioned and directed by Directive 4 and Directive 7. Here is a 12 July 1995 report from the Main Staff to Karadzic, describing the situation in the corps: "All the Corps units are at the highest level of combat-readiness and are doing everything to ensure that there are no surprises. The units engaged in carrying out the Krivaja 95 task are carrying out all the combat tasks according to plan." And it goes on to specify some of the activities and then it continues regarding the situation in the territory: "In the Drina Corps zone of responsibility, the population is being taken from the Srebrenica enclave to Kladanj in an organised manner. It is estimated that on this day there are about 10.000 Muslims to be transported." Meanwhile, Your Honours, the Bosnian Serb army and Bosnian Serb police forces completed the separation of the men and boys in Potocari, that is, the approximately 1.000 to 2.000 men and boys, and transported them to Bratunac, the immediately adjacent municipality just a few kilometres away, this on July 13th. Now, turning to the other group of men and boys I referred to, that larger group, those who had gathered at Susnjari and began to flee toward Muslim-held territory in Tuzla, that same day, on July 13th, thousands of these men were captured or surrendered to Bosnian Serb army or Bosnian Serb police forces. I want to show you a clip of men from the column surrendering, a video that was filmed by a Serb journalist accompanying a Bosnian police commander, and you will see a man being forced to call to his son and to other Muslims in the column to surrender, and then you will see men from the column surrendering.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Come down here. I'm down here, Nermin" -- [French on English channel] -- with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, we are hearing French again. Yes. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Nermin, come down here. I'm down here. It's safe to come to the Serbs. Come on. They all should come. Nermin, come down here, it's safe. I'm with the Serbs. Come all of you, as many as there are of you. "I don't know, from some desert. "How much time did you spend there? "We spent two days and two nights, completely surrounded. "Well, where are your rifles? "I didn't have a rifle. I did not. I'm a civilian. "A civilian? "Sure. I don't fight. "Are you very afraid? "How could I not be afraid. "Come on, man, don't be scared. What are you afraid of, for fuck's sake? Come on, come on, have no fear."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that man being forced to call to his son was a man named Ramo Osmanovic. His remains were found in a mass grave. His teenage son, Nermin, to whom Ramo was forced to call with the promise "it's safe to come to the Serbs," his remains were found in a mass grave as well. By the afternoon of 13 July, the Bosnian Serb army, the Bosnian Serb police forces had custody of approximately 5 to 6.000 Muslim prisoners at three main points along the road that you saw on the map earlier, that was Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and Sandici. Throughout the operation, the supreme commander, Radovan Karadzic, was kept abreast of the activities in and around Srebrenica, including the large-scale surrender of Muslim men from the column. On the night of 13 July, the VRS sent an "urgent" report to Karadzic which stated the following: "The enemy from the former enclave of Srebrenica is in a state of total disarray, and the troops are surrendering in large numbers to the VRS." And as you will learn, VRS reports to Karadzic over the following days also notified him of the capture of Muslims by the VRS. But let me remain focus on the 13th. On the afternoon of the 13th, approximately 1.000 Muslim prisoners who had surrendered or had been captured were bussed or marched from Sandici to the nearby Kravica warehouse. And at that warehouse, these prisoners were executed by Bosnian Serb army and Bosnian Serb police forces. Other organised execution were carried out on that day by police forces at Jadar River and Sandici meadow. During the late afternoon and early evening -- evening hours of 13th July, the remaining prisoners captured along the road were transported to Bratunac where they were detained in buildings, trucks, buses throughout the town along with the other Muslim men who had been separated from their families in Potocari. These thousands of prisoners were detained in appalling conditions on the night of the 13th, without food, without medical attention, with insufficient water. Many were killed right in the centre of Bratunac. Many more were beaten savagely. And meanwhile, the supreme commander continued to be kept abreast of events. I mentioned earlier the regular reports he received, but he was also in direct contact with General Mladic. That evening, on the 13th of July, at about the time that the very last Muslims were being bussed and trucked out of the enclave by the Bosnian Serb army, Bosnian Serb police and civilian authorities, Karadzic, from his office in Pale, spoke with Mladic for approximately an hour on a speakerphone. Their conversation was cordial throughout. One witness to the conversation overheard them discussing the promotion of Radislav Krstic, who was convicting of aiding and abetting genocide. Another witness will testify that Mladic reported to Karadzic that "Srebrenica was done." And that "Zepa was next." Again, this call took place at approximately the time of the departure of the last buses removing the remaining women and children, the last Muslims in Srebrenica. As Mladic reported to Karadzic, Srebrenica was done. Thus, the evidence is clear that the command chain functioned as it was intended to during this period, with Mladic and other elements of the VRS reporting to the supreme commander. And on the 13th, that supreme commander, Karadzic, was aware that mass expulsions had been underway, that Srebrenica was "done," that large numbers of Muslim male prisoners had been captured. And he would also speak to his hand-picked new civilian commissioner for the Serb municipality of Srebrenica that evening, that's Miroslav Deronjic. Deronjic could have made that call from his office, but in a moment of fortuitous historical irony, Deronjic left his office and went to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters in an effort to keep the call as secret as possible. What he didn't know is that military transmissions were less secure than the telephone landline he had in his office. And as a result, we know that Karadzic not only knew about the prisoners but ordered their transfer out of Bratunac, out of Bratunac which was in uncomfortable proximity to the internationals, indeed close enough so that internationals were able to hear shots as you'll see in one DutchBat report. During that conversation, Karadzic asked: "... how many thousands?" "The President is asking how many thousands?" "Deronjic: About two for the time being." And this intercepted conversation, Your Honours, takes place through an intermediary. Deronjic is talking to someone who is speaking to Karadzic. Deronjic can hear Karadzic on the other end. "About two for the time being. "Two, Mr. President (heard in the background). "Deronjic: But there will be more during the night." And Karadzic told him what should be done with these prisoners. "Deronjic, the President says: 'All the goods must be placed inside the warehouses before 12.00 tomorrow. "Deronjic: Right. "Deronjic, not in the warehouses over there, but somewhere else." That is, Your Honours, somewhere other than Bratunac. Now, although Karadzic tried to mask this conversation using code, warehouses, goods, he cannot hide what it reveals. He knew that Muslim prisoners were being held in Bratunac and he ordered them moved to warehouses elsewhere, and that is exactly what happened. Starting that night, shortly after the conclusion of this call and continuing on to the next morning, the prisoners were transferred from Bratunac to temporary detention facilities in Zvornik or around Zvornik, where they were held prior to their execution. Over the course of the next 72 hours they were all, but for a miraculous handful of survivors, murdered. Your Honours, you will hear evidence from those survivors and what they went through, waiting for hours underneath piles of bodies, feigning death, until they were able to make their escape. Now, bear in mind that while this slaughter was taking place, the VRS-run camp in Batkovic, that's in Bijeljina, was still functioning more than three years after Mladic had established it to handle the surplus of civilians who were then being cleansed from their homes. It had the facilities to handle thousands of prisoners. Just 60 kilometres away from Zvornik by asphalt road, Batkovic was the place that captured prisoners should have been sent were they to be held as prisoners or exchanged. But that is not where the Muslim men in Bratunac went. They were sent to the Zvornik area because they were not going to be exchanged, but because they were going to be killed. Your Honours, you will hear that Miroslav Deronjic has suggested that Karadzic intended that the Bratunac prisoners be sent to Batkovic to protect them, but that is belied by the evidence. Not only did Karadzic order the prisoners sent to warehouses rather than to the Batkovic camp, not only were prisoners in fact sent to schools and other makeshift detention facilities as ordered by Karadzic, but Karadzic then sought to ensure that the mass killings would not be known as they were happening and afterward. But before I address Karadzic's efforts to ensure that the mass killings remain hidden, let me point you to some additional discussions that he had that preceded those efforts. You will learn, for example, that the next day, on the 14th of July, Deronjic met with Karadzic in the president's office in Pale and spoke with him about the killings in the Kravica warehouse. Later that same day, on the 14th, after meeting with Deronjic, Karadzic met with an American visitor, Bob Djurdjevic, together they watched televised CNN and SkyNews coverage of the situation in Srebrenica. Karadzic, speaking to Djurdjevic, took credit for Directive 7 and the attack on Srebrenica, and in Djurdjevic's contemporaneous notes of the meeting he wrote: "RK," Karadzic, "said that the attacks on Srebrenica and Zepa were a part of what he called 'my order number 7.' He said that their objective is 'to raise the temperature to the boiling point.'" And during this meeting Karadzic also received a phone call from one of his field commanders from Srebrenica regarding military action around Konjevic Polje and Kasaba. And this call was yet another of the sources of information that kept the supreme commander, the man who had ordered the operation, informed throughout, and is yet one more example beyond the regular reports, beyond Mladic, beyond Karadzic's civilian commissioner, beyond direct calls from military commanders in the field, Karadzic also received information on the situation on the ground from the police and state security. In this intercept of the 16th of July, 1995, a Bosnian Serb army Main Staff duty officer tells Mladic that Karadzic has just called from the -- has just called the Bosnian Serb army Main Staff because Karadzic had received information from the Bosnian Serb police, and specifically from the head of state security, that the Zvornik Brigade commander had opened a corridor in the VRS lines through which Muslims from the column were passing through to Muslim-held territory. "The President called a short while ago. He said he had been informed by Karisik," that's the head of state security, "that Pandurevic had arranged passage for the Muslims over to that territory." And I'll discuss a bit later how this information about the escape of Muslims angered Karadzic. So what did the supreme commander do with the knowledge that Muslim men were being seized, detained, and murdered? He attempted to ensure the operation's continuing success through false assurances to an increasingly suspicious international media and to an increasingly alarmed international community. From the very start of the Srebrenica operation until well after the world knew about the mass killings, Karadzic covered up what was happening or had taken place. He insisted that the Muslim population had "left voluntarily," and he lied to the media regarding the captured and executed Muslim men and boys. By the night of the 13th of July, 1995, as I've described, Karadzic had full knowledge of the forcible transfer of the population. He knew of the thousands of Muslim men detained in Bratunac and had ordered that they be transferred to warehouses. And later that same night, at around 2130 hours, Karadzic gave an interview to a journalist for the Spanish newspaper El Pais. When asked about Srebrenica Karadzic stated: "Srebrenica is now free. "Unfortunately, very few Muslims may stay in Srebrenica, because now they are aware that Srebrenica is going to belong to the Serbian state, and since it is clear Muslims want to live in a Muslim state and they expressed their own willingness to -- to go to the Muslim state, to the part of Bosnia that is under Muslim control and is going to be Muslim state or Muslim-Croat federation." He went on to deny allegations of ethnic cleansing, stating: "Anyone who wanted to stay could stay." He stated that in full confidence, of course, that the media did not have access to, for example, Directive 4, ordering the cleansing of the enclaves, or Directive 7, ordering "an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants." Four days later Karadzic was interviewed again, this time by British journalist David Frost. This interview took place as the victims of the killing operations in Zvornik were being buried in mass graves. When asked whether he felt he may have made a mistake in taking Srebrenica given the immense scale of international condemnation, Karadzic replied: "Not at all," and justified his view with the comment that Srebrenica had not been a safe area but a stronghold. When asked by Frost to explain the allegations that 15.000 men from Srebrenica were missing or unaccounted for, Karadzic denied that there were missing men other than those in the column who were still en route to Tuzla. And here's a portion of that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "The question of the numbers of people who were found or whatever. What about the figures we've read in the media, your favourite area, in the media about 15.000 men missing, unaccounted for, from Srebrenica and that you have got them somewhere? That's what we read. That's? "Well, even yesterday and today we have opened our own lines and many of them have entered Muslim territory. Many of them have been combatants and our local commander has allowed them to pass through our territory, and they are passing even tonight. Many of them are in the forests and they are trying to get Muslim-controlled territory and we are not interfering. We don't want to fight with them because they do not intend to take our territory. They want to leave our territory. "And there are not 15.000 men from Srebrenica missing? "No, absolutely not. Many of them have joined their own people. Yesterday and today and even tomorrow, there will be many more of them passing through Serbian lines."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And here's what actually happened, Your Honour, and was happening. I won't attempt to describe in detail the horror of the meticulous execution of over 7.000 men and boys which took place over those days; I'll merely give a very brief listing of the largest organised killings. On the 13th of July, Kravica warehouse, approximately 1.000 executed with automatic rifles and hand-grenades. Over the next days, 14 July through 16 July, Orahovac school and in the nearby fields, approximately 1.000 executed. The Petkovici school and the dam, on the afternoon and evening of 14 July and during the early-morning hours of 15 July 1995, approximately 1.000 executed. Rocevic school and Kozluk, over 1.000 executed, several at Rocevic and over a thousand at Kozluk. I want to show you some photos of those victims after they were exhumed from that area. The first you'll see is of the mass grave or a mass grave. The second. Next, please. You see the blindfold. Next, please. A man with his hands tied behind his back. Next. Your Honours, you'll hear evidence - and if we return to that slide, please - you'll hear evidence that the Muslim victims in Kozluk clutched at weeds and shrubbery as they were executed along the banks of the Drina River, and you can see that depicted in this photo. And continuing the terrible litany of executions, Kula school near Pilica, Branjevo Farm, several executed at the school, the remaining approximately 1200 executed at Branjevo Farm. And this is a photograph depicting some of the bodies at Branjevo Farm. Pilica cultural centre, approximately 500 executed. Your Honours, these large-scale killings required enormous resources; trucks, ammunition, heavy machinery for burials, thousands of litres of fuel, as well as significant manpower to secure the detention and execution sites and to carry out the actual executions and burials. They were carried out quickly and efficiently and required a high degree of planning and coordination between the Bosnian Serb army, the Bosnian Serb police, and the civilian authorities, all of whom were involved. The list of those who knew and who had to know is long, from Mladic and Tolimir and others on the Main Staff, the officers and soldiers of the Drina Corps, the officers and soldiers of the Zvornik, Bratunac, and other brigades of the Drina Corps, the Ministry of the Interior, the subordinates of the Ministry of the Interior, and above all - above all - the supreme commander. In addition to these large-scale killings, Your Honours, around this time-period there were organised killings of a lesser scale but nevertheless significant, at Jadar River, Cerska valley, Sandici, the Luke School near Tisca, Snagovo, Trnovo, and Bisina, and sporadic killings of Muslim men continued past July, as the VRS's own reports show, after the 17th of July, Muslim stragglers were hunted down and executed on the spot around Srebrenica and Zepa. Throughout this time, from directly after the fall of Srebrenica onwards, mainstream media reports were circulating about the massive ethnic cleansing at Srebrenica and the indications that mass murder had been committed by Bosnian Serb forces. On the 17th of July, 1995, the same day as Frost's interview with Karadzic, a British newspaper reported on the piles of corpses in front of the Kravica warehouse. The headline of that article is: "Bodies pile up in horror of Srebrenica." And that same day, 17 July, Studio B Television in Belgrade aired the actual video, a video of the pile of bodies outside the Kravica warehouse. I'll show you that video. You'll see it first quite quickly and then it will be replayed for you in slow motion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Hello, how are you. What's up? "There are dead Muslim soldiers and ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Can you see that, for fuck's sake? "No one's here on the line."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yet Karadzic continued to issue denials of any crimes by Bosnian Serb forces in Srebrenica. When asked months later by a CNN reporter about the allegations of massive crimes in Srebrenica and the need for an investigation, Karadzic insisted that he had already initiated an investigation of his own. He claimed that UNPROFOR had monitored the whole operation and that there was "no mass killing or any killing." By this time, thousands of bodies of victims had been dug up and transferred to secondary graves by the VRS, the MUP, and civilian authorities in an attempt to cover up the crime. I would like to show you this clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "You say that you're for an investigation or any kind of trial concerning alleged atrocities. What about the unanswered questions concerning Srebrenica? Will there be conducted some kind of investigation? Would you pledge such an investigation? "I have already ordered the investigation about any allegation and among them about Srebrenica. I was reported that the UNPROFOR people has monitored the whole affair. There was no killing, mass killing, or any killing; that Muslims have checked many more refugees in Srebrenica in order to get more help for their own army."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Earlier, Your Honours, I directed your attention to Karadzic's words to the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 6th of August, 1995, during which he praised and took credit for the Srebrenica operation. I'll direct your attention to those again, this time on a slide. "The time had come and I signed Directive 7 to capture Teocak, Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. The directive was signed and we embarked on it. I was in favour of all the decisions that we made and I support them. All the decisions are recorded in the Supreme Command. I ordered in verbal and written form to attack Zepa and Srebrenica." And he added that they had not been able to take Gorazde at that time but: "... there will be the right time to take Gorazde, just as there was the right time to conquer Srebrenica. There will be the right time to attack and destroy Gorazde." On other occasions he singled out commanders of the operation for praise, particularly Krstic. This was an interview on August 4th, 1995: "Now, Krstic, for instance, who planned it in front of me and I approved that task for Srebrenica, who did it exceptionally well. Of course the Main Staff, Mladic and all others help, but it should be known that Krstic is a great army commander." Your Honours, the only concern that Karadzic ever expressed about Srebrenica was that one of his commanders had let some of the Muslims escape. He was angry that some of the Muslims had gotten away. This is how Karadzic described the escape, as he called it -- escape of, excuse me, as he called them, the Turks, their escape to Muslim-held territory. And this is what he said at the Bosnian Serb Assembly: "9.000 armed Turks in the woods and mountains could have taken Srebrenica again. They could have burned Milici, Vlasenica, and Zvornik. People from that area can tell you all about it because it could have happened if they were smart enough and if they had a command. It is a landing division with 9.000 men. It could have been a landing operation. Only our men and dear God could save us. About 50 to 60 of our men got killed there trying to block them, but several thousand of soldiers eventually managed to pass and now Srebrenica division has been formed, lined up in Tuzla and ordered to get back to Srebrenica. We were not able to surround and destroy that enemy because we were in a hurry to get to Zepa, and we assigned two generals to Zepa to waste 15 days in negotiations with jackasses and idiots who were wasting their time instead of letting Rajko Kusic finish all of it, or maybe General Krstic who proved to be very good."
